lesson.title: When Categories Move Together: Detecting Association
lesson.summary: Two categorical variables show association when their conditional distributions differ meaningfully across categories, a pattern you can spot by comparing distributions but never taken alone as proof of cause and effect.
lesson.body:
Two categorical variables are said to show an association when the conditional distribution of one variable changes depending on which category of the other variable you condition on. If knowing an individual's grade level changes what you would predict about their phone operating system, the two variables are associated. If knowing the grade level tells you nothing new, meaning the conditional distributions all look basically the same, the variables show no meaningful association, sometimes described as roughly independent. Notice that this definition is built entirely out of tools you already have: two-way tables to organize the counts, and conditional distributions to compare across categories.

This gives you a clear baseline to compare against. If grade level truly had nothing to do with operating system choice, you would expect the conditional distribution of operating system among freshmen, the conditional distribution among sophomores, and the overall marginal distribution of operating system to all be approximately equal. Any noticeable gap between those conditional distributions and the marginal distribution is evidence pointing toward association rather than independence. Small gaps of a percentage point or two are common even when two variables are genuinely unrelated, simply because of the randomness in who happened to be surveyed, so the size of the gap matters as much as its mere existence.

Return to the student survey: the marginal distribution of operating system across all 300 students is 53.3 percent iPhone. But conditioned on freshman, the figure rises to 58.3 percent iPhone, and conditioned on sophomore, it falls to exactly 50 percent iPhone. An 8.3 percentage point gap between the freshman and sophomore conditional distributions, pulling away from the 53.3 percent overall figure in opposite directions, is a real pattern, not identical distributions, so this sample shows some association between grade level and operating system choice.

A segmented bar graph, where each bar represents one category of the explanatory variable and is divided proportionally by the response variable's categories, makes this same comparison visible at a glance: bars of noticeably different proportions signal association, while bars that look like near identical copies of each other signal little or none. One caution is essential, though: finding an association only tells you the two variables move together in this sample, not that one causes the other. A third, unmeasured variable, called a confounding variable, could be driving both, and ruling that out requires far more than a two-way table.

Once you suspect two variables are associated, a natural next question is which one plays the role of predictor and which plays the role of outcome, the distinction that the explanatory variable and response variable ideas exist to sort out, and which shapes how you would eventually design a study to investigate the relationship more rigorously.
